title: US private credit: fast growth, redemption limits and more loans not paying interest
event_started: 2026 (default rate reported at or above 6.0% since April 2026)
what_happened: US private credit has grown to about $1.5 trillion outstanding, up 13.8% in a year. The Federal Reserve reports that some funds kept redemption limits and net flows stayed negative. At the two largest listed lenders, loans that have stopped paying interest stood at 2.4% and 2.9% of the portfolio at cost on 2026-09-30, up from earlier in the year.
how_it_reaches_markets: Losses at business development companies, banks and insurers that lend to or hold private credit; redemption pressure on non-traded funds; tighter credit for mid-sized companies.

sourced_facts.text: Federal Reserve Financial Stability Report (November 2026): private credit outstanding $1,504 billion, up 13.8% from 2025:Q2 to 2026:Q2 (Table 1.1)
Same report: 'Redemption requests at certain business development companies trended lower, though funds maintained redemption limits and net flows remained negative.'

Federal Reserve staff note, 2026-11-09: U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles held about $1.9 trillion in assets at the end of 2025; BDCs 'tend to be more highly levered with an average debt-to-equity ratio around 1'

Same report (Overview): 'private companies and public firms with lower credit ratings demonstrated weaker debt-servicing capacity'. The report gives no private credit default rate in the part we could read word for word

Ares Capital, results for 2026-09-30 (filed with the SEC, 2026-10-27): loans on non-accrual status were 2.4% of total investments at amortized cost (1.4% at fair value), against 1.8% (1.2%) on 2025-12-31; portfolio $29.2 billion at fair value

Blue Owl Capital Corporation, results for 2026-09-30 (filed with the SEC, 2026-11-04): investments on non-accrual were 2.9% of the portfolio at cost (0.8% at fair value), against 2.8% (0.8%) on 2026-06-30; portfolio $15.1 billion at fair value

resolved_when_all: Loans on non-accrual are 1.8% or less of the portfolio at cost at both Ares Capital and Blue Owl Capital Corporation in two quarterly reports in a row
Credit stress component of this ledger is Moderate or lower throughout the same period
worsened_when_any: Loans on non-accrual reach 3.5% or more of the portfolio at cost at either Ares Capital or Blue Owl Capital Corporation
A large private credit fund suspends or limits redemptions, or a bank discloses a private-credit-related loss above 1 billion dollars
Credit stress component of this ledger reaches High

superseded_sources.reason: Source rule of 2026-11-26: at least one primary source per card; commentary, blogs and reposts are not used as support
facts_as_first_written: Fitch: 6.2% trailing-12-month default rate to October 2026, 6.3% in September; 90 unique defaulters; 10.7% for issuers under 25 million dollars EBITDA versus 2.4% above 100 million (Max's Digest, 2026-11-18)
JPMorgan forecasts leveraged-loan defaults of 4.5% in 2027 and 4.75% in 2028 (Max's Digest)
Moody's: banks had extended nearly 300 billion dollars to private credit funds, BDCs and CLOs as of October 2025 (Forbes, 2026-05-24)
No fund redemption gate in November 2026 is stated in these sources
superseded_sources.summary_as_first_written: The Fitch trailing-12-month US private credit default rate stood at 6.2% in October 2026. Most default events are payment deferrals and maturity extensions rather than bankruptcies, and smaller borrowers default far more often. Banks and life insurers have large exposures to private credit funds.

notes: Added 2026-11-28: 'non-accrual' loans are loans on which the lender has stopped booking interest because it doubts it will be paid. The figure is read from each company's quarterly results as filed with the SEC, as a share of the portfolio at amortized cost. Ares Capital and Blue Owl Capital Corporation are used because they are the two largest listed lenders of this kind (business development companies). 1.8% is where Ares stood at the end of 2025. 'Large private credit fund' means one with at least $1 billion in assets.
The Fitch default rate named in the first version is still listed under unconfirmed facts as background. It no longer decides anything on this card.

counter_view.note: The strongest reason this card's reading may be wrong. AFMX's own judgment, using the facts listed on the card.
counter_view.text: Stress has not shown up in traded credit: the high-yield spread in this record is at 1 of 3 steps. The Federal Reserve reports that redemption requests have trended lower. The two lenders we count are the largest and may be the best run; trouble among small borrowers could stay there, or could be building where these two numbers do not show it.

forecasts.basis: The default rate is reported at 6.2% and would have to be under 4.0% for three months. One fund of $1 billion or more newly limiting redemptions is enough to worsen the card, and limits already exist at some funds.

Written because the default-rate conditions changed on 2026-11-28. Both lenders would need two quarterly reports at 1.8% or less from 2.4% and 2.9%, and at most two reports arrive before the deadline. One fund of $1 billion or more newly limiting redemptions is still enough to worsen the card. Forecast 1 stays scored against the conditions as first written.
